item.text: {"question_id":"6B.5","answer":"During 2023, Tshisekedi’s administration had formal measurement and accountability arrangements: the CPVS monitored presidential commitments, the education ministry held an annual performance review, the PDL-145T government described a citizen project-tracking tool, and budget rules required performance indicators, reporting, internal controls, independent and objective internal audit, external audit participation, and publication of budget-execution information (BATCH-0020-E011; BATCH-0023-E006; BATCH-0023-E003; BATCH-0029-E004; BATCH-0029-E005). These materials establish monitoring intent, institutional safeguards, and some government or externally commissioned evaluation, but do not by themselves establish credible published welfare data, effective independent scrutiny, or completed corrective action. The WFP/UNICEF/FAO evaluation found dedicated monitoring teams but limited coordination, only 50% of planned activities fully implemented, and recommended redesign and better alignment; it does not attribute the shortcomings or subsequent response personally to Tshisekedi (BATCH-0002-E004). A government-commissioned review of the state of siege and presidential acknowledgment of declining purchasing power show some recognition of problems, but no supplied evidence demonstrates that the review produced changes or that the acknowledgment led to effective welfare correction (BATCH-0021-E012; BATCH-0015-E004). Evidence of audit and scrutiny was mixed: an official finance audit led to suspension of 12 logging concessions but not cancellation of all illegal permits; the National Commission on Human Rights issued reports and followed complaints, while authorities denied UN access to some detention facilities and the institutions struggled with effectiveness (BATCH-0001-E009; BATCH-0011-E014). Parliamentary and Court of Accounts observations later identified incoherent and noncompliant spending, overruns, uncertified debts, and budgeted works without visible field action, while the World Bank reported that dissolution of the Social Fund paused disbursements during transition arrangements (BATCH-0024-E003; BATCH-0024-E004; BATCH-0017-E002). Related evidence that CENI rejected independent electoral-roll auditing and that few prior reform recommendations were implemented is not welfare-program evidence directly, but qualifies the broader claim of openness to independent review and correction; attribution is institutional rather than personal (BATCH-0013-E009; BATCH-0013-E010). Overall, the record supports monitoring structures and some audits or evaluations, but documented, ruler-attributed correction of failed welfare design, implementation, or personnel remains limited and
